Cost Estimators use drawings, bills of quantities, and market prices to calculate labor, material, equipment, and indirect costs for construction or manufacturing projects. They prepare bid and budget estimates, analyze risk, and inform commercial decisions.

paragraphs: In the morning, estimators calculate quantities from new drawings and apply local standards and line items. After lunch, they verify unit prices and consult purchasing when an item rises sharply. In the afternoon, they add labor and equipment costs, produce the total, and document risks. Before leaving, they benchmark historical data and prepare for the next day's bid presentation.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 221,400 Cost Estimators were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to decline to 212,100 by 2034, a net loss of about 9,300 jobs, with about 16,900 openings annually. The median annual wage was about $77,100 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace Cost Estimators, but it will accelerate quantity takeoffs and pricing. BIM takeoffs, price databases, and automated quotes speed up repetitive work. Estimators shift from processing line items to risk judgment, negotiation strategy, commercial decisions, and historical benchmarking. Pure takeoff and pricing work faces pressure, while people with commercial judgment and accountability become more valuable.
